messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan is a 30-year-old carpenter who came to treatment after months of insisting to his wife that he could “handle it” and then finding that more and more of his day was organized around not being caught off guard. The event he witnessed happened on a renovation job last year. He had been working beside another contractor using a table saw when the man’s hand was pulled into the blade. Ethan saw the sudden opening of flesh, the blood on the wood, and the look on the man’s face before anyone had fully understood what had happened. He remembered trying to grab him and press down with rags while other workers shouted for help. What stayed with him was not a coherent story he could tell from beginning to end, but flashes of torn skin, the warmth and pressure of contact, and the metallic, sickening taste that seemed to rise in his mouth while he crouched there. Even in early sessions, he would stop and say he did not know how to explain it; the worst part seemed to live in his body more than in words.

In the weeks after, Ethan returned to work, but ordinary moments on job sites began to undo him. If a coworker clapped him on the shoulder from behind, if he caught an unexpected taste in his mouth that reminded him of that day, or if he noticed a cut or fresh wound on someone’s hand, the whole scene came back without warning. He did not simply remember it. For a few seconds it felt fully present again, as if he were back on the floor with blood on his hands, hearing the noise and feeling the panic all at once. Those moments left him scrambling to get away from his own mind. He would head for the break area and eat whatever he could find, fast and past fullness, because the heaviness of food dulled him. At other times he would go blank on purpose, staring fixedly and trying to leave his body until he felt far away. He also began cutting off thoughts before they formed, treating any drift toward the incident as dangerous.

What frightened Ethan almost as much as the intrusions was what they seemed to say about him. Each time a trigger dropped him back into the memory, he came away thinking that something in him had been permanently damaged. He had always seen himself as steady, practical, the kind of man others could count on in a crisis, and now he was ashamed by how quickly touch, a taste, or the sight of an injury could shake him. He had come to believe he could no longer rely on himself; if his mind could betray him this easily at work, then his life as he knew it had been destroyed. Those conclusions made him scan even more warily for danger in daily life. On construction sites he watched other men’s hands, knuckles, and forearms before he heard what they were saying, and he stiffened when anyone moved close enough to touch him, already bracing for the next hit of memory.

Over time the loop tightened. Because he was so convinced the trauma had changed him for the worse, any return of the memory felt like proof rather than symptom. He would struggle to put the experience into words and then take that failure as further evidence that he was broken beyond repair. The more he judged himself this way, the more potent the triggers seemed to become; even a minor scrape on a coworker’s wrist could seize his attention and pull the sensory reliving into the foreground. Once the memory took over, he would eat to the point of discomfort, disappear into a deliberate fog, or force his thoughts elsewhere, and afterward he despised himself for needing those measures. To Ethan, that pattern confirmed that he was no longer the man he had been.

The cost has spread beyond the job. His wife has noticed how he pulls away from casual touch and how often he retreats after work to eat in silence rather than sit with her. At work he has become less confident around others, especially when tools are out and someone has a nick or cut, and he worries that his hesitation is visible. He finally sought help after freezing on a site when a younger worker sliced his palm with a utility knife; at the sight of the blood, Ethan was instantly back in the original accident and then spent the rest of the day trying not to think, eating continuously from the vending machine, and feeling himself go numb. He came in saying he was afraid this was permanent and that if he could not trust his own mind, he might lose his marriage and the trade he has built his life around. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to be able to stand on a job site, be touched unexpectedly, see an injury, and remain in the present instead of disappearing.
